basic_info.about: Reshma Saujani is a leading activist, the founder of Girls Who Code, the founder and CEO of Moms First, and the host of My So-Called Midlife with Lemonada Media. She has spent more than a decade building movements to fight for women and girls’ economic empowerment, working to close the gender gap in the tech sector, and most recently fighting for the structural changes moms need and deserve including affordable child care and paid leave. She is a New York Times bestselling author of several books including PAY UP: The Future of Women and Work (And Why It’s Different Than You Think), Brave, Not Perfect, and the Girls Who Code book series. As a leading voice on women’s empowerment, her 2023 Smith College Commencement speech on imposter syndrome has more than 18 million views, and her influential TED talk, “Teach girls bravery, not perfection,” has more than 54 million views globally. In 2024, she launched My So-Called Midlife, a podcast with Lemonada Media that quickly entered Apple’s Top 10 show chart, reached #1 in Health and Fitness, and was named one of the best new podcasts of the year by TIME magazine. Reshma began her career as an attorney and Democratic organizer. In 2010, she surged onto the political scene as the first Indian American woman to run for U.S. Congress. Reshma lives in New York City with her husband, Nihal, their sons, Shaan and Sai, and their dog Steve.

experience.description: Girls Who Code is a non-profit organization working to close the gender gap in technology and change the image of what a programmer looks like and does. With their 7-week Summer Immersion Program, a 2-week specialized Campus Program, afterschool Clubs, and a 13-book New York Times best-selling series, they are leading the movement to inspire, educate, and equip young women with the computing skills to pursue 21st-century opportunities. Girls Who Code will have reached over 185,000 girls in all 50 states and several US territories. To join the movement or learn more, visit girlswhocode.com.

One of the best career moves for men is to have children (the make on average 6% more per child) while for women it’s the worst career move (they make 4% less per child). 

Shelley J. Correll, a sociology professor at Stanford University found that employers were less likely to call back a woman if she was a mother and offered $11,000 less than childless women and $13,000 less than fathers. 

On the other hand, men *with kids were more likely to get a call back than men *without* kids. That’s why there’s a motherhood penalty but a fatherhood bonus, and that this mom tax is five times higher for for low-income women. 

One thing men can do to remedy this is to take on more parenting and talk about it in the workplace. When a mother leaves early she’s assumed to leave for childcare while when a man leaves early he’s assumed to leave for a work-related event. Men need to be open and honest about the role they’re taking in the home. 

The most effective way to minimize these draconian inequalities is paid parental leave and universal child care, something we should all unite for ✊❤️

Thank you @emilybaldoni and all the other moms who are tenaciously fighting for a world that no longer punishes mothers for raising all of us. @justinbaldoni @jamey_heath_ ❤️

For the past decade, I told young women to lean in real hard and girlboss their way to the top. I was wrong.

I’ve been sitting with this title for a long time. No Country for Mothers.

Say it out loud. You already know it’s true.

American moms have asked ourselves for years why motherhood is so hard in this country. Why we’re exhausted. Why we’re blamed. Why nothing ever seems to change no matter how loud we get. So we did something about it. 

We teamed up with @culturehousemedia and we made a film to find out. 

No Country for Mothers is the documentary I wish existed before I became a mom. It’s the reckoning we deserve. And it’s finally here.

Watch the trailer, then comment MOTHERS below and I’ll send everything straight to your DMs. Screenings are coming to a city near you.
Let’s go. 🎬

Gender relations in the U.S. are broken — this is how I think we can fix it. 

It starts by recognizing the big con: that progress is a zero-sum game. Here’s what I mean:

“They’ve built a world where men and women don’t talk to each other, don’t see each other, don’t trust each other. Disconnection isn’t just the consequence — it’s the goal. Because if we don’t see each other, we won’t stand up for each other… The story that you’ve been told: that power is a pie and you got to fight for your slice, that’s a lie. They got you so busy fighting a gender war to keep you from fighting a class war.”

It shouldn’t take an economics degree to understand this: parents cannot work without childcare.

Which makes childcare an economic issue.

But we have spent decades treating it like a personal problem mothers are supposed to solve alone. And then blame them for stepping back from work instead of asking why the system failed them.

#NoCountryforMothers breaks down the economic pressures forcing women into impossible choices and why that policy failure keeps getting pinned on moms.

Bring your community to help move the conversation forward. Host a watch party or find one near you at the link in bio.

🇺🇸 What if a film could become the starting point for a movement?
Reshma Saujani, founder of @girlswhocode and @momsfirstus, shared how “No Country for Mothers” uses documentary storytelling to bring mothers' experiences to the center and create spaces for collective action.
More than a film to watch, it becomes a conversation communities can take part in.
Where do stories and communities meet? 💬

🇮🇹 E se un film potesse diventare il punto di partenza per un movimento?
Reshma Saujani, founder di @girlswhocode e @momsfirstus, ha raccontato come “No Country for Mothers” utilizzi il documentario per mettere al centro le esperienze delle madri e creare spazi di azione collettiva.
Più che un film da guardare, diventa una conversazione di cui le comunità possono fare parte.
Dove si incontrano storie e comunità? 💬

Of course nobody could name the most powerful woman in tech. We spent four years dismantling the rooms she’d be standing in.

Read the full investigation from @laurengoode at @WIRED, link in my stories.

Motherhood is still the unfinished business of feminism.

Too many mothers are still forced to choose between their families and economic security — without paid leave, affordable childcare, or the support to make either choice sustainable.

We made #NoCountryforMothers to show what happens when motherhood is left out of the fight for equality, and why that has to change.

The film is not available to stream because it is meant to be watched in community. Find a screening near you (or host one yourself!) at the link in bio.

We screened part of No Country for Mothers at the Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health (@columbiapublichealth), and the conversation afterward was exactly why we made this film.

Huge thank you to Lauren Houghton, who organized the evening on behalf of Mailman and joined me on the panel. Her Free Time 4 Wellness study is showing what every mom already knows: give a mother free childcare and she finally has time for her own health. Lauren is turning that into data a policymaker or a CEO can’t ignore, and I’m so grateful she brought us into her work.

And thank you to Emmy Liss, who leads NYC’s Mayor’s Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education (@nycchildcare) and is one of the people delivering universal childcare in this city. Listening to her talk about what it actually takes to deliver reminded me that this is completely possible when leaders decide to do it.

Many thanks also to Dean Jonathan Mermin for welcoming us, Randi Hutter Epstein for moderating, and the whole Mailman team for a beautiful night.

In 2024, the Surgeon General called parental stress an urgent public health issue. How can we expect mothers to take care of their own health when we make it so hard to take care of their kids? Research, policy, and advocacy each get us part of the way there. Put them in the same room and you start to see how we actually win.

You can’t stream No Country for Mothers anywhere. The only way to see it is at a community screening, so find one near you or host your own at the 🔗.

This is one of the most dangerous times to be an American woman.

And still, we are being told that women are the reason men are struggling. That women have too much power. That pulling women back is the way forward.

They want us fighting each other, but #NoCountryforMothers is about seeing through that distraction, and coming together to demand the support mothers, fathers, and families deserve.

The film is screening nationwide right now. It is not on streaming or on demand because this conversation is meant to happen in community. Host or find a screening near you at the link in bio.
